title: Medicines, doses and formulations
intro: A plain-language guide to the medicines used for gender-affirming hormone therapy in Australia: what each one is, what forms it comes in, and the ranges Australian prescribers work within. It is background reading, not a prescription. Blood tests, fertility, PrEP and surgery are on the [Monitoring and related care](#/monitoring) page.

sections.h: Start here: the dose is yours, and only your prescriber sets it
body: Every number on this page is a typical range that Australian prescribers work within. None of it is a recommendation for you.

Two people on the same medicine can be on very different doses and both be right. It depends on your goals, your blood results, your other health conditions, your age, and what your body does with the medicine.

Guidance is explicit that doses are individualised, and that some people — including many non-binary people — deliberately aim for partial effects on a lower dose. Low dose is not no dose, and it is a legitimate goal to raise with your prescriber [1][2].
list: Only a prescriber can set your dose, and only a prescriber should change it
Never start, stop, increase or skip a dose on your own
If your dose is not working for you, that is a conversation — not a change to make at home
Your pharmacist can talk it through with you for free, without an appointment
sections.note: If you are reading this to work out whether your own dose is right, the answer is not on this page. Take the question to your prescriber or your pharmacist.

body: Estradiol is the oestrogen used in feminising hormone therapy in Australia. It is the same hormone a body makes naturally, given as a medicine.
It comes as tablets, skin patches and skin gel. Which one suits you is a clinical decision, not just a preference.
Patches and gel avoid the first pass through the liver, so they are preferred where the risk of blood clots is higher [1].
Ethinylestradiol, the oestrogen in the combined pill, is not used for gender affirmation. The high doses used until 1989 were linked to more clots [1].

Estradiol injections and implants are not available as registered products here. Compounded versions exist, but they are not tested for potency, efficacy, safety or quality control, and Australian guidance advises caution [1].

Australia's 2026 standards of care say implants are not recommended for starting therapy, but are preferred by many people for maintenance, once treatment is settled. They often give higher oestradiol levels. They come only from pharmacies that make and sterilise them, private fees apply, and blood tests are used to time the next implant. Their clot risk is not known [3].
list: Tablets — estradiol valerate (Progynova) or estradiol (Zumenon), commonly 2–8 mg daily, taken once a day or split into two doses [4]. Other guidance: the 2019 position statement gives 2–6 mg daily [1], and the Zumenon product information, written for menopause, uses one 2 mg tablet a day [5]
Tablets under the tongue — changes how the medicine is absorbed, so only do this if your prescriber has told you to [6]

Patches — Estradot or Estraderm MX, changed twice a week. Australian guidance gives a common range of 50–200 micrograms per 24 hours; many prescribers start low and build up every two to three months, which may mean wearing more than one patch at a time [4]

Gel — once daily, measured in pumps or sachets. Australian guidance gives one to four pumps of Estrogel (0.75 mg estradiol each) or one to two 1 g Sandrena sachets daily [4]. Other guidance: the Estrogel product information, written for menopause, says the long-term safety of more than two pumps a day has not been established [7]
Monitoring — oestradiol and total testosterone, rechecked six to eight weeks after any change [8]
sections.note: Estradiol tablets and patches are on the PBS with no restriction attached, so the usual co-payment applies. Both estradiol gels, Sandrena sachets and the Estrogel pump, are listed too [9][10].

Gel: put it on your skin every day.
Your doctor picks the form and the dose.

body: These medicines lower the effect of testosterone. Oestrogen on its own does not usually suppress testosterone enough, so a blocker is often added.

Two are used in Australia: spironolactone and cyproterone acetate. There is no good head-to-head evidence that one is better than the other, so the choice comes down to your health history and how you tolerate it [1].

The advice is to use the lowest effective dose of cyproterone. The Australian product information reports meningioma with long-term use at doses of 25 mg a day and above, with the risk rising as the total dose taken over the years adds up. If a meningioma is diagnosed, cyproterone must be stopped permanently. Prolactinoma has also been reported [1][11].

Bicalutamide, a prostate cancer medicine, is sometimes used as a blocker. Australia's 2026 standards of care say it should not be a first choice, because there is very little evidence for it in gender-affirming care [12]. Liver damage, liver failure and lung damage, including deaths, have been reported, so anyone taking it needs regular liver blood tests for as long as they take it [12]. The Australian product information says most liver changes happen in the first 6 months, and that it is stopped for jaundice or if the liver test ALT rises above twice the upper limit of normal [13]. In July 2026 it added a warning about interstitial lung disease, a lung inflammation that has caused deaths. Bicalutamide is stopped if this is diagnosed [13, 14]. It can make warfarin work more strongly, so anyone on warfarin needs closer INR blood tests, and in rare cases it can make skin burn more easily in the sun [13].

After an orchidectomy a blocker is no longer needed [1]. Whether to stop hormones before an operation is covered in [Hormones around surgery](#/monitoring#sec-monitoring-5) on the Monitoring and related care page.
list: Spironolactone (Spiractin, Aldactone and generics) — a daily tablet, usually 50–200 mg daily in Australian guidance [4], and 100–200 mg in the 2019 position statement [1]
Spironolactone monitoring — it is also a diuretic, so blood tests check electrolytes and kidney function, along with your blood pressure [8]
Cyproterone acetate (Androcur, Anterone, Cyproterone Sandoz) — a stronger blocker, and a progestogen in its own right. Australian guidance gives 12.5 mg once a week up to 25 mg daily [4]
Cyproterone, lower still — 12.5 mg (a quarter tablet) every second day or twice a week is commonly used [4]
Cyproterone monitoring — blood tests usually include liver function [8]
Finasteride and dutasteride are not general blockers; they are commonly added for scalp hair loss, although Australian guidance notes it is unclear whether they add benefit [4]
sections.note: Spironolactone and potassium interact. Tell your pharmacist about any potassium supplements, salt substitutes or blood pressure medicines before you start.

body: A separate group of hormones that some people take alongside oestrogen. If one is used, Australia's 2026 standards of care prefer micronised progesterone (for example Prometrium) [4].
The evidence for whether progestogens add anything to breast development or mood is limited, which is why practice varies between prescribers. It is a reasonable thing to ask about.

They are also used the other way around. If periods continue on testosterone and cause distress, the options include raising the testosterone dose, an oral progestogen, or a progestogen-releasing IUD [1].
list: Micronised progesterone (Prometrium) — commonly 100–200 mg nightly, reviewed after three to six months [4]
No progesterone blood level target is given [4]

body: Testosterone is the medicine used in masculinising hormone therapy. In Australia it comes as a long-acting intramuscular injection, a daily gel, a daily cream, and shorter-acting injections [15].
The gels and cream suit a daily routine, or a dose adjusted in smaller steps. The long-acting injection is given by a clinician every few months.
Testosterone implants (pellets) are used by a small number of people. They last several months, but they are not PBS-subsidised and can only be made by a compounding pharmacy [15].
On the PBS, every testosterone product needs an Authority prescription. Your prescriber arranges that before you get to the pharmacy [16][17].

**Why does testosterone need a PBS Authority?** Every PBS testosterone product is listed as Authority Required [18][19]. For gender-affirming care, the prescriber needs a one-off second opinion from an endocrinologist, urologist or sexual health physician. It can be in person or by telehealth, and that specialist's name is then used on later scripts. A script can also be written once an appointment with the specialist is booked [19]. The [Authority wording card](#/clinician-guide) explains the wording for prescribers and pharmacists.

**Which testosterone injections are there?** The long-acting testosterone undecanoate injection, 1,000 mg in 4 mL, is on the PBS under four brands: Reandron 1000, Gonadron, Rejunon 1000 and Testosterone ADVZ 1000 [18]. Two shorter-acting injections, Primoteston Depot and Sustanon 250, are not PBS-subsidised [19].

**Are there testosterone patches?** Not at present. The TGA cancelled the Androderm testosterone patches at the sponsor's request: the 12.2 mg patch from 29 June 2022 and the 24.3 mg patch from 26 June 2025 [20][21]. Australia's 2026 standards of care list testosterone as gels, a cream and injections [19].

**Can testosterone be an e-script?** Electronic prescriptions can be used for any medicine anywhere in Australia, and you can still ask for a paper script. An e-script arrives as a token, usually a QR code, by SMS or email [22].
list: Testosterone undecanoate (Reandron 1000, and newer brands including Gonadron and Rejunon 1000) — 1,000 mg in 4 mL, deep intramuscular. A second dose about six weeks after the first, then one every 10 to 14 weeks [1][8][23]

Testosterone 1% gel (Testogel) — a metered pump delivering 12.5 mg per press, or 5 g sachets, applied daily. Australian standards give one to eight pumps, or one to two sachets, daily; four pumps is often enough for full masculinisation [4][17]
Testosterone 2% gel (Testavan), 23 mg per press, one to three presses daily, and 5% cream (AndroForte 5), 1–4 mL daily, often 2 mL [4][17]

Shorter-acting esters — testosterone enantate (Primoteston Depot) and Sustanon, usually 125–250 mg every two to four weeks [4]. Primoteston Depot was removed from the PBS on 1 February 2018 at the manufacturer's request and is now a private prescription [24]; Sustanon is not PBS-subsidised either [17][25]
Monitoring — trough total testosterone and haematocrit; see the [blood tests section](#/monitoring#sec-monitoring-0) on the Monitoring and related care page [1][8]
sections.note: Testosterone can harm a developing pregnancy and does not reliably stop ovulation. If pregnancy is possible for you, contraception is worth a specific conversation with your prescriber — do not assume testosterone covers it [1].

body: These medicines pause puberty by switching off the signal from the brain that drives it. They are given as an implant or a depot injection, always under specialist care.

Australia's standards of care for children and adolescents name goserelin (Zoladex), leuprorelin (Lucrin, Eligard) and triptorelin (Diphereline), repeated every one to six months, depending on the product [26].

Since 1 October 2026, triptorelin 3.75 mg (Diphereline), a monthly injection, has been on the PBS with no restriction (item 9378N), but its listing carries a note that it "is not for use in gender dysphoria in minors" [27]. So, like goserelin and leuprorelin, which are PBS-listed only for other conditions, it is a private prescription for puberty suppression. SA Health's model of care (2023) notes that a young person who cannot get them through a hospital faces a cost of several thousand dollars a year [28].

Access to goserelin has been changing. The 3.6 mg implant was due to leave the PBS on 1 November 2026, with a free Zoladex Continuity Program planned in its place [29]. On 23 September 2026 the sponsor, AstraZeneca, said instead that the implant will stay on the PBS until 1 May 2027, that PBS prescriptions written by 30 April 2027 can be filled until 1 May 2028, and that the Continuity Program will not go ahead [30]. The TGA shortage record still shows the earlier date [31], but goserelin is not on the PBS list of deletions for 1 November 2026 [32]. If this affects you or your child, ask your prescriber and your pharmacist well before the next dose is due.

sections.h: If your medicine is hard to get
body: Shortages happen, and estradiol patches have been the long-running one. The 25, 50, 75 and 100 microgram Estradot patches are still in short supply, with the TGA estimating a return to normal supply by 31 December 2026; the [supply page](#/supply) shows the latest position [33].

The TGA has approved substitution for these patches, so where it is appropriate your pharmacist can supply a different brand or strength that delivers the same amount of estradiol per day, without a new prescription. That approval runs to 28 February 2027 [34].
Ask your pharmacist what is available and whether the product they can get is PBS-subsidised. Bring it up before you run out, not on your last day of supply.

International guidance is explicit that established hormone therapy should be continued rather than stopped, including through periods when your mental health is poor, unless there is a medical reason to stop [2]. Continuity is part of the treatment.

sections.h: Other medicines used alongside hormone therapy
body: Some effects of hormone therapy have their own treatments: a topical retinoid with benzoyl peroxide, doxycycline or isotretinoin for acne [25]; topical minoxidil [35] or finasteride [36] for scalp hair loss; norethisterone [37], medroxyprogesterone acetate [38] or a levonorgestrel IUD [39] for periods that continue on testosterone [15]; and low-dose vaginal oestrogen for vaginal dryness [40]. They are not hormone therapy in a different form, and none is automatic [8][4].
The [add-on therapies page](#/add-on-therapies) explains each one: why the effect happens, what is usually tried first, and what to ask your prescriber.
